# Dynamic Cache Probing Strategy Migration Guide

## Preserve the Old Entry Point First

This work initially located files by issue name and call name, eventually landing on `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`. At present, the only content that can be directly verified in the file header is this line:

```js
import { pick } from '../utils/core.js';
```

It shows that `configuration_utils.js` has a direct dependency from `../utils/core.js`. It does not show that `DynamicCache` is created here, nor does it list the callers. The v1 working hypothesis—that dynamic caching and the cache probing strategy might share an entry point in this area—remains as a historical assessment, but is no longer treated as evidence that migration is complete.

The first thing to migrate, therefore, is the verification order: change from “an issue name or call name points to a file” to “capture the observed state first, then check back against local declarations in the file”. The input provides neither a new target file nor specific callers or command names. A path that has not yet been provided must not be filled in as the migration destination.

## Observed State Before Migration

Before the check begins, the working directory must contain no old cache and no personal configuration. This condition ensures that “newly created” and “not newly created” remain two distinguishable observations. If the directory already contains an old cache, seeing an existing path does not show that this check created it; if personal configuration changes the default behavior, an identical record from another environment cannot be directly placed alongside this result either.

During preparation, record only the conditions, without writing conclusions in advance. The record can begin like this:

```text
Old cache: None / Unconfirmed
Personal configuration: None / Unconfirmed
DynamicCache: Awaiting observation
Cache probing strategy: Awaiting check
```

“Unconfirmed” must not be written as “None”. If the preparation conditions themselves were not recorded, file inspection may still continue, but this result must be kept separate from the baseline that satisfies the conditions. Cleaning the working directory is preparation for the next round of checks, and must not retroactively become evidence that “the check left no remnants”.

## First Branch: DynamicCache

The `DynamicCache` branch only answers whether the cache object or its corresponding path has changed. Preserve three cases when observing: newly created, not newly created, and different results between two checks. The third case must not be reduced to “cache present”, because it shows that the same observation did not yield the same result under different conditions.

This branch is not responsible for explaining the probing check's exit result or for establishing the source-code entry point. Even if a newly created path is observed, it can only be recorded as an observation; the file must not be identified as the creator merely because an earlier investigation pointed to `configuration_utils.js`. Conversely, if no file changes are observed, that must not be used to state that the cache was not used: no file changes and no cache activity are not the same observation.

When recording DynamicCache, at least place the observation target and its result together, rather than leaving an isolated word:

```text
Observation target: DynamicCache
Result: Newly created / Not newly created / Different from the previous check
Working-directory file changes: Record separately, do not include in the result above
```

Here, “working-directory file changes” still describes the observed state; it is not another way of writing the DynamicCache result. Only when both items are recorded can a later comparison determine whether “cache object changes” and “directory changes” occurred together; if only one item is available, the other remains unrecorded.

## Second Branch: Cache Probing Strategy

Check the cache probing strategy separately, rather than combining it with the first branch into a single “cache is normal” result. The actual command for this check does not appear in the frozen materials, so recording the check name is sufficient when documenting the entry point; do not invent commands, arguments, or exit codes.

This branch must preserve three distinct results: the exit code, file changes in the working directory, and residual directories after the check completes. The exit code only indicates the check process's return result; it cannot replace directory observations. Directory changes do not mean the check failed either, and residual directories must be recorded separately by name or as “present/absent”; if the materials do not provide specific directory names, do not invent them.

The observed state can be saved in exactly the following order:

```text
Cache probing strategy
  Exit code: To be recorded
  File changes: To be recorded
  Residual directories: To be recorded
```

If only the exit code is available, mark the other two items as unrecorded; if only a clean working directory is observed, the exit code must not be filled in as successful either. In particular, the directory state after cleanup must not be treated as its state immediately after the check simply because cleanup took place after the check. To compare before and after migration, all three observations must retain their respective positions in time.

## Do Not Merge the Two Paths

The current verification order can be drawn as a branching path:

```text
No old cache, no personal configuration
              |
        Record preparation conditions
          /           \
Observe DynamicCache       Check cache probing strategy
Newly created/Not newly created/Result changed      Exit code
                          File changes
                          Residual directories
          \             /
             Review the local file
                 |
configuration_utils.js + pick dependency
```

There is only one shared prerequisite before the split, and each branch preserves its own results afterward. When the branches rejoin, only compare them; do not combine them into a single conclusion. For example, DynamicCache not being newly created does not automatically mean the probing strategy left no residual directories; a normal probing exit result does not automatically mean DynamicCache must have been newly created either. The materials provide no causal relationship between these two items.

If only one branch is completed during the check, leave the other branch's fields blank in the document. Completing the DynamicCache observation does not mean the cache probing strategy has been verified; completing the probing check does not mean the old file entry point has explained the cache behavior either. Recording it this way preserves the differences needed for the next comparison better than entering a single “compatible” result.

## Migrate from the Old Path to an Observation-First Order

The advantage of the old path is that it makes the file easy to find. Its drawback is equally specific: an issue name and call name can lead someone to a relevant file, but cannot independently prove that the object is created by that file. The new order does not remove the old path; it places it after the observations.

First, confirm the environment conditions and register empty fields for DynamicCache and the probing check. Second, perform the two observations and save their results separately. Third, return to `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js` and verify only the currently visible local declarations and the `pick` dependency. Fourth, place the observations and the file's adjacent relationships side by side; if there is insufficient material to connect them, stop at side-by-side records rather than extending them into a call chain.

This has another practical benefit: when new results conflict with an old assessment, it becomes clear whether the conflict is at the observation level or the file-location level. If the observation of DynamicCache changes while the file header still contains only the same direct dependency, that change cannot be interpreted as a change in which file is responsible. If the file entry point can still be found but the probing check leaves different residual directories, the file's existence cannot be recorded as evidence that behavior is unchanged either.

“Migration” here means migrating the verification entry point and recording order, not that source-code relocation has already been completed. New implementation paths, caller lists, and specific recovery commands do not appear in the materials, so this page does not assume they exist.

## Incorporating Existing Baselines

HFJ-209 recorded `baseline_recorded` on 2025-09-23. This record is suitable as a starting point for comparison: later observations must not overwrite it and then pass off the new results as the original baseline. At a minimum, the baseline must retain the conditions and observations actually written down at the time; do not infer the result of DynamicCache from the action name “baseline_recorded”.

By 2025-09-26, the action for HFJ-209 had changed to `work_started`. What can be confirmed here is that verification had moved from baseline recording into the working phase; this cannot be used to fill in the probing exit code, file changes, or residual directories. If these results were obtained later, create a separate observation record and place it alongside the baseline.

When incorporating these records, distinguish the purposes of the two points in time:

```text
baseline_recorded
  Purpose: Mark the starting point for comparison

work_started
  Purpose: Mark the start of continued verification

Subsequent observations
  Purpose: Fill in the actual observations for both branches
```

Action names are not behavioral results. They can help reconstruct the order of records, but cannot replace engineering facts such as whether a cache was newly created or whether probing left directories behind. If the baseline recorded only DynamicCache, do not backfill it from a later probing check; if the baseline did not record the environment conditions, do not assume it necessarily used a clean directory either.

## Boundaries of Caller Compatibility

The materials do not provide specific callers, new files after migration, or integration points in external projects. This page therefore specifies only the level of observation detail that callers must support: if a caller reproduces DynamicCache, it should distinguish newly created, not newly created, and changed results; if a caller performs a probing check, it should separately preserve the exit code, file changes, and residual directories.

This is not proof that callers have completed the switch. When a caller returns only final success or failure, at least directory and residual information is lost, so the result cannot be directly compared with the old baseline. When a caller reports only that the directory was unchanged, that also cannot be used to assert that no cache activity occurred. If such a difference arises, save the original output first, then identify which item is missing.

Do not extend the file-header dependency in `configuration_utils.js` into an end-to-end relationship. Currently, all that is known is that `pick` is a direct dependency; it is not known who calls the file or whether it receives or creates DynamicCache. If new code snippets become available later, place them under the corresponding local branch; a new name must not substitute for the full reference relationship.

## Fall Back to the Old Entry Point

When the new order cannot be followed, falling back means locating the original file again, not deleting observations already captured. If checking back still leads to `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`, retain the `pick` dependency in the file header as a local anchor, and note alongside it which observation was not completed.

If DynamicCache has already been observed but the cache probing strategy has not yet been checked, return only to the second branch; do not mark the second branch as passed just because the first has a result. If neither branch has results, return to environment preparation and establish the baseline again. If the probing check has been completed but the residual-directory record is missing, fill in only that item when falling back; do not substitute the post-cleanup directory state for the original observation.

Restoring the old path only guarantees that the original local entry point can still be found; it does not guarantee that the v1 working hypothesis holds again. The file located by the old investigation can still be referenced, but must not be promoted to a conclusion that “the implementation is here”. Preserving the old file-change, exit-code, and residual-directory records is also important; the next check needs to know which materials came from the previous round and which are new observations.

## Conclusions Currently Retained

The following can be confirmed: observing DynamicCache and checking the cache probing strategy should remain separate; the old-cache and personal-configuration conditions must be made explicit before checking; the probing branch separately records the exit code, working-directory file changes, and residual directories; the old investigation can be traced back to `packages/transformers/src/generation/configuration_utils.js`, whose file header directly shows the `pick` dependency; HFJ-209 first recorded a baseline and then entered the working phase.

The unconfirmed points are also retained: whether this file creates DynamicCache, whether a new migration target file exists, which callers have switched, whether the probing strategy has a consistent result across environments, and whether the baseline included all environment conditions at the time. Subsequent materials should go in the corresponding observation, source-code, or caller sections. Without new materials, do not combine these gaps into a single compatibility conclusion.

The former asks whether the model object can make it to a writable result; the latter asks whether the file list ultimately returned by the invocation entry point preserves the expected order. Combining the two into a single “export passed” record loses working-directory side effects and makes it impossible to tell whether the order changed at the listing stage or the write-to-disk stage.

The trace-back starting point is still `packages/transformers/src/utils/tensor.js`. title: OCR Mapping Cache-Key Decision

versions.body:
# OCR Mapping Cache-Key Decision

When we put the OCR mapping and cache-key shape into the same requirements check, the reason was simple: before model loading, both surfaced as “a name or state doesn’t match.” This consolidation made troubleshooting easier, but it wasn’t appropriate to plan implementation on that basis. When a name doesn’t resolve to a loadable model, the cache-shape result can’t show that the mapping has been completed; when a cache record’s key doesn’t match what the caller expects, that can’t be used to infer which item is missing from the model directory.

The initial working hypothesis was that both issues might be caused by the same omitted model declaration. To check this, the record retained only `packages/transformers/src/models/trocr/modeling_trocr.js` as the adjacent entry that had been opened at the time. It helps return to the local declaration, but the path name alone can’t establish that the OCR mapping, model directory, and cache state belong to the same implementation location. This counterexample invalidated the original judgment that “one change would close both out.”

Three approaches were compared at the time.

- Combine the two issues into one change ticket and close it only after both the mapping and cache checks pass.
- Fill in the model name first, then treat the cache shape as a follow-on validation of that change.
- Keep two acceptance points separate: verify the mapping against the model-type-to-constructor result, and verify the cache by whether the named key can be consumed.

The third approach was chosen. This doesn’t mean the two have no runtime relationship; it avoids using a green result on one side as sign-off for the other. The OCR item records only whether the model type, task entry point, and export name are consistent; the cache item records only whether the naming, index, and shape of each layer’s state can still be read. If a single change touches both, the commit description can mention them together, but the regression record must identify separately which acceptance point failed.

The proposal to have OCR model files generate the cache-key description uniformly was also deferred at the time. Model mapping is a directory-level choice, while cache keys come from state layout; putting the latter into the mapping table would make the name table responsible for explaining runtime structure, making the scope of changes harder to determine when hybrid attention layers are added. The cache-key description should stay near the code that actually consumes the state, while model mapping should retain a searchable type-to-constructor relationship.

This page preserves an old framing that now looks too narrow: it once treated the OCR mapping solely as a single missing-name issue and did not record entry-point differences after the model family expanded. It is still useful for understanding why acceptance was split at the time, but it should not be treated as a complete model-directory rule. On subsequent checks, first confirm the registration result for the specific model type, then check whether the corresponding cache key is still read by the caller.

## Mapping and Key Boundary

Model-family names locate registration entries; cache keys describe runtime state. Even when they appear together, verify each one against its own evidence.

# Nemotron and Olmo Issue Troubleshooting Tree

Nemotron and Olmo are reviewed together in the pre-release checks because both fall within the scope of issues that occur after model loading; this does not mean they share an implementation, and the test result for one model cannot be treated as a conclusion about the other.

First, record where the error occurs:

```text
Error occurs
├─ Before model type or constructor selection
│  └─ Record the model type from the configuration and the call entry point; do not change the test fixture
├─ During model loading
│  └─ Distinguish the download, weight opening, and construction stages
└─ While an existing model instance is running
   └─ Record the input shape, location of the first output, and whether the cleanup stage was reached
```

The Olmo2 entry that can currently be reviewed directly is `packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js`. The file imports `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM` from `../../../src/transformers.js`, and imports `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME`, `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME`, `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME`, and `DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS` from `../../init.js`. First check whether the failure occurred in the test section for loading, execution, or release. Do not classify it as the same kind of loading issue just because Olmo appears in the logs.

Earlier notes placed Nemotron alongside this test entry only to make tracking easier. There is no local test anchor for Nemotron here yet. If the issue can only be attributed to Nemotron, stop at the model-selection and constructor entry points, and record the actual file location hit separately; do not turn the Olmo2 test case into substitute evidence for Nemotron.

When a rerun is needed, keep the same set of `DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS`, obtain one complete result first, and then narrow it down to a single model. If the complete result times out only during the release phase, inspect the path corresponding to `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` first; do not write it up as an inference failure. If the loading phase ends but the execution phase is never entered, retain the location where loading ended and the name of the subsequent test that was not entered.

Not yet confirmed: whether the two types of issues in the pre-release package share an upstream entry point; which existing test file should contain Nemotron's minimal reproduction.

# Nemotron and Olmo Anomaly Troubleshooting Tree

This record originally placed Nemotron and Olmo side by side under a single troubleshooting entry point. That worked for catching scattered anomaly names that appeared during the pre-release phase, but a later review required separating “the same verification pass” from “the same implementation path.” The former still holds; the latter cannot be inferred from the existing material.

The file that can currently be reviewed directly is `packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js`. Its name, imported objects, and test time limit are sufficient to show that it is a local follow-up checkpoint for Olmo2; it cannot fill in the missing test relationship for Nemotron. During handling, first lay out the anomalies by stage, then decide whether to enter this file. Do not jump directly to “shared failure” based on similar model names, being in the same pre-release version, or appearing in the same regression pass.

The practice left in the earlier records was: open the Olmo2 tests first, then look for the construction stage after seeing the model import. This practice can still be used to locate symptoms on the Olmo side, but it cannot serve as Nemotron’s first step. The original branches are retained below, with the stopping points later found to be necessary added after each branch.

```text
An anomaly related to Nemotron or Olmo is received
|
+-- 1. First ask: At what stage did the anomaly occur?
|   |
|   +-- Before model type resolution, model selection, or constructor retrieval
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   +-- Record the model type, configuration snippet, and actual call entry point
|   |   |   +-- Do not open the Olmo2 tests as a substitute for this entry point
|   |   |   `-- If there is no entry-point location, stop attribution and retain the symptom only
|   |
|   +-- During model loading
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Distinguish file retrieval, weight opening, and object creation
|   |   +-- On the Olmo side, you can switch to the loading section in the Olmo2 tests
|   |   `-- On the Nemotron side, first find its own matching construction or test location
|   |
|   +-- The model instance has been created; the anomaly occurs during execution
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Record the input shape, first failure location, and whether output already exists
|   |   +-- Do not record a subsequent cleanup timeout as an execution failure
|   |   `-- Narrow the input only when the issue is reproducible
|   |
|   `-- Anomaly during release or destruction
|       |
|       +-- List it separately as a cleanup stage
|       `-- Do not modify the model mapping to handle release issues
|
`-- 2. Keep Nemotron and Olmo records separate
    |
    +-- Olmo: The Olmo2 tests can be used as a local entry point
    `-- Nemotron: Wait for the file or call location that actually matches
```

## Clarify the symptoms first

“Exception boundaries” here is not the name of an error category. It refers to several boundaries that must not be crossed during troubleshooting: between the model directory and the specific constructor, between loading and execution, between execution and release, and between Olmo's existing test entry points and Nemotron's unknown entry points. If a report says only “model failure”, outputs from different stages can easily be combined into a single issue later.

When a record comes in, first capture just four brief details: whether a model instance had already been obtained before the error appeared; whether an execution had already been entered; whether any output appeared; and whether the test or call reached release. Without these four details, do not guess the stage from the model name. They are not intended to form a complete incident report, but to prevent a loading failure from being treated as a runtime failure, or a timeout during release from being interpreted as a lack of model support.

If the caller can identify the model type or constructor entry point, record the type name and entry-point location exactly as given. Do not infer and add registry relationships based on the name when no entry point is provided. Both Nemotron and Olmo may be mentioned before model selection, but “mentioned” does not mean selection has been completed.

If the caller provides only a test name, first confirm whether that test name corresponds to a model, processor, tokenizer, or shared initialization. A name containing Olmo does not necessarily mean the failure occurred in the model object itself; likewise, a name containing Nemotron does not establish that the exception came from the model directory. First find the first section of code actually entered, then use the name as a supporting clue.

## Olmo-side entry points

`packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js` is the currently visible location of the Olmo2 tests. The file imports directly from `../../../src/transformers.js`:

```js
import { GPT2Tokenizer, Olmo2ForCausalLM } from "../../../src/transformers.js";
```

This import answers a very narrow question: at this point, the test file uses both `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM`. It cannot, on its own, answer which model was ultimately selected at runtime, which files were loaded, or whether a particular exception was caused by the tokenizer. Therefore, during troubleshooting, do not copy the import list into a model support matrix.

For Olmo reports, the first step is to check whether the exception occurred before or after these imported objects were used. If the test could not proceed around import or initialization, record that location and the complete error; do not start by reducing the generation input. Only if the model object has already been created should you proceed to inspect the execution section. If execution has returned and the test finally gets stuck during release, move to the cleanup branch; do not go back and revise the model-selection hypothesis.

The file also takes these time limits and default options from `../../init.js`:

```js
import {
  MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME,
  MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME,
  MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME,
  DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS,
} from "../../init.js";
```

The three time-limit names here provide a division into stages, not the cause of an exception. `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME` is suitable only for marking the wait boundary during loading; `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME` is suitable for marking the execution boundary after the model starts working; `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` reminds us that release comes after execution. When a test takes a long time, first check which boundary it falls near. Do not attribute it directly to model loading simply because the total duration is long.

`DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS` should also be retained in the record as the fact that “the test defaults were used for this run”; do not expand it into a parameter list that has not been seen. When comparing options, use the overrides visible at the actual call site as the basis. If there are no overrides, do not write that a particular switch caused the difference.

For the Olmo branch, proceed in the following order:

1. Confirm whether the record refers to the Olmo or Olmo2 test entry point. The two must not be treated as interchangeable on this page.
2. Open `test_modeling_olmo2.js` and first find where the imported object is first used in the test.
3. Mark whether the exception occurs during model loading, during test execution, or before resource cleanup.
4. If tokenization results are involved, separately note whether `GPT2Tokenizer` has been used; do not assume it is the cause just because it appears in the import list.
5. If a model object is involved, separately note whether `Olmo2ForCausalLM` has finished being created.
6. Only when the issue can be reproduced reliably at the same stage should you narrow it down further with a smaller input or a single test case.

Step 4 and step 5 must not be combined into “model initialization”. A tokenizer having been called before the model is created and the first execution failing after model creation are two different troubleshooting paths. Combining them into one will leave subsequent records unable to explain which object was actually reached.

### Olmo Loading Stage

If the exception occurs during loading, first confirm whether creation of the model object has started. The test file is known to import `Olmo2ForCausalLM`, but the import statement itself is not evidence that creation succeeded. In the record, you can use stage descriptions such as “reached the import”, “entered the loading call”, or “failed after object creation”; do not collapse all three into “loading failed”.

If the exception occurs before the model object is obtained, retain the call entry point and the error, and do not change the timeout constant in the test. The timeout constant is only a test-side boundary; it cannot establish which part of upstream selection, file reading, or object creation went wrong.

If object creation starts but does not finish, still classify it as loading. Do not minimize the execution input at this point, because execution has not yet begun. If you change the defaults for troubleshooting, you must distinguish the “original defaults” from the “temporary overrides” in the record; otherwise, later results cannot be assessed to determine whether they reflect the original issue.

If a loading attempt stops near `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME`, this only indicates that the loading stage crossed that test boundary. It does not mean that the network, weights, cache, or constructor has been confirmed as the cause. When investigating further, follow only the objects actually traversed by the current call; do not list storage, transport, or cache implementations that were not reached as candidates on this page.

### Olmo Execution Stage

Enter the execution phase only after the object has been created. Keep only the minimal input characteristics here: whether the input is empty, whether it is a single item, and whether the first failure occurred before any output was produced. Do not fill in sequence length, device, filename, or return value just to make the record look complete; when that information was not observed at the scene, writing it with precision will only mislead the next reproduction attempt.

If `GPT2Tokenizer` has completed its local work, but execution of `Olmo2ForCausalLM` has still not returned, record “tokenizer passed” and “model execution has not returned” separately. The former narrows down the current path; the latter still does not indicate whether the problem is in model computation, input preparation, or the call wrapper.

If an execution result has already appeared and the failure occurs afterward during finalization, return to the release branch. Do not rewrite an execution phase that has already succeeded as “unstable”. A successful execution and a failed release can occur in the same run, and they should be preserved as two separate facts.

`MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME` is used to identify the boundary of the test execution phase. When it is exceeded, record which test step was actually entered and whether any output had already appeared. Do not combine it with `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME` into a generic “model timeout”; doing so would lose the most useful phase information.

### Olmo release phase

Resource release occurs after model execution. If an exception occurs around release or destruction, first confirm whether execution output already exists, then check whether cleanup has just begun. Since the test file uses `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` separately, the record should also preserve this phase as a separate line.

When an exception occurs during the release phase, do not modify the model mapping, replace the tokenizer, or switch the model constructor to another model just to get a passing run. Those actions would change earlier phases and obscure the execution that had already completed. You can first reduce the test to a single case that goes through release; if that single case still cannot identify the specific cleanup location, stop at “exception during the release phase” and wait for the actual call location.

## Nemotron-side entry point

The most common mistake in combined Nemotron and Olmo records is to put Nemotron into the same test case after seeing an Olmo2 test. The available material does not provide Nemotron’s corresponding test file, import declaration, or specific call edge. Therefore, Nemotron’s starting point must be the model selection, constructor, or test location actually encountered in the report, rather than a copy of the Olmo2 test configuration.

If a Nemotron report is received, first distinguish between the following two situations:

- The report provides a model type, constructor name, or call location: use that location to determine whether the problem occurs before selection, during loading, during execution, or during release.
- The report only says “Nемotron exception” without an actual location: record only the symptoms and environment differences; do not escalate it to an Olmo2 regression or claim that a runnable minimal test case already exists.

Here, “environment differences” refers only to directly observable differences, such as whether a prerelease package was used in the same record, whether the call came from a test or an application, and whether the release phase was reached. Do not attach a version number, runner, or platform name when no actual value is available. The prerelease version itself is not a common cause.

If Nemotron fails before model selection, the most important thing right now is to preserve the model type and the entry point the request reached. At this stage, there is no reason yet to move into Olmo model testing. If selection has completed but construction has not, continue tracing the path Nemotron actually reached; still do not substitute the creation process for `Olmo2ForCausalLM` for that path.

If Nemotron has completed creation and fails during execution, record the minimal characteristics of the input and whether output has started. If it subsequently fails only during resource release, log it under the cleanup stage. Even if the stage names are the same as Olmo's, keep separate reproduction entries for the two sides; what they share is a classification scheme, not evidence.

The stopping condition for the Nemotron branch comes earlier than for Olmo: without a locally reached location, do not keep guessing about model files, tokenizers, configuration fields, or shared storage. You can leave a pending item after the exception record: an actual construction or test entry point that was reached is needed. Do not disguise this pending item as an already verified regression conclusion.

## Correction to the Early Decision to Merge

The original record described “Nemotron and Olmo are both within the exception boundary” in terms that were too closely aligned, making it easy to read them as the same type of defect. That assessment retains its purpose at the time: when scattered prerelease issues appeared, on-call staff would at least not overlook either name. The handling is now revised as follows:

- The two model names can be used together as search clues.
- The Olmo2 test file is only for localized follow-up checks on the Olmo side.
- Nemotron must first have its own actual entry point identified.
- If an exception has no stage, add the stage first; if it has no entry point, stop at the missing entry point first.

This does not remove Nemotron from the scope of investigation; it removes it from an unverified shared path. If the two sides are later found to have the same call site, a shared branch can then be established at that site; until then, similar symptoms must not be used to merge evidence.

## Handling Order

The following order applies to a new report. It deliberately does not require running through every item; first, place the current exception in a branch that will not mislead anyone.

**A. Identify the model side first.** If the report explicitly concerns Olmo, enter the Olmo branch; if it explicitly concerns Nemotron, enter the Nemotron branch; if it only refers generically to a model exception, do not attribute it to either side. When the model side is unclear, find the call entry point first, rather than picking a seemingly similar case from the test directory.

**B. Identify the stage next.** Prefer the four categories “pre-selection, loading, execution, release.” Pre-selection covers model type resolution, selection, and the period before obtaining the constructor; loading runs from the start of model creation until the model object is usable; execution runs from when the object is usable until output exists or execution returns; release runs from the start of cleanup until resource release is complete. If the boundary is temporarily unclear, you can write “undetermined between loading/execution,” but do not force it into one category.

**C. Decide whether to narrow it down last.** Narrowing down to a single case is worthwhile only when both the model side and the stage are known. For Olmo loading, execution, and release, you can continue examining the existing objects in the test file; for Nemotron, narrow it down only when an actual reached location is already known. The goal of narrowing it down is to confirm the stage, not to get a successful run on a different path as quickly as possible.

**D. Close out the record.** You can stop once you have the stage, the entry point, and the original error. If an entry point is missing, state the specific gap: Nemotron's actual test or construction entry point has not yet been located; or the first failure location within the Olmo2 test has not yet been located. Do not replace these two distinct gaps with a generic “further analysis needed.”

## Common wrong turns

### Treating a successful import as proof that the model is usable

The fact that `test_modeling_olmo2.js` can import `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM` does not mean the test has finished creating the model object, nor does it mean execution succeeded. After import completes, the process may still stop during loading, execution, or release. If the record only says “import is fine,” the next person handling it still will not know the failure stage.

The correction is to add the first actual failure point after import. If you cannot obtain that point, retain “not yet located after import”; do not upgrade it to “model is usable.”

### Treating a test time limit as the root cause

The three time limits correspond to loading, execution, and release, respectively. They help identify the stage, but do not indicate the cause. This is especially true of `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME`: when this boundary is reached, the preceding model execution may already have completed. Classifying it as model loading will direct subsequent changes to the wrong place.

The correction is to first check the last completed stage. If creation has completed, no longer call it “unable to load”; if output has been obtained, no longer call it “unable to execute.” Describe the remaining problem according to its actual stage.

### Directly reusing the Olmo2 test case for Nemotron

This is the most dangerous shortcut in the early records. The Olmo2 file is an existing entry point for a specific case, not a universal fixture for all language models. Copying that test case for Nemotron, even if it produces a new result, cannot establish that it follows the same path as the original Nemotron exception.

The correction is to first find the actual Nemotron match. Stop if you cannot find it; do not borrow Olmo2's imports, time limits, or default options to manufacture a conclusion. You can put the Olmo investigation record and the Nemotron record awaiting localization on the same page, but they must remain two separate tracks.

### Recasting a release problem as an execution problem

When a model call has already returned and a resource cleanup exception occurs afterward, the easiest approach is often to retain only the final failure text. This loses the counterevidence that “execution has already completed.” For prerelease regressions, this distinction affects whether to inspect the model path or shutdown handling.

The correction is to write down two short conclusions together: whether execution returned; whether release completed. Do not let the latter overwrite the former for the sake of brevity.

### Changing the default options before confirming the original problem

`DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS` is the source of the default options currently used by the test file. Changing it directly without first preserving the original option state only yields a run result under different conditions. Especially when the boundary between loading and execution is unclear, this can make the original exception disappear without establishing that the problem has been fixed.

The correction is to run the original call first, then make one local change within the same stage. If the problem disappears after the change, you can only record “the temporary override changed the result”; unless you can locate the actual overridden option and stage, do not write it as a definitive attribution.

## Short notes you can leave directly while on call

The following sentences can be used as appropriate for the situation; not all of them need to be filled in:

- “Olmo2: Model import has been reached; it is not confirmed whether object creation has been entered.”
- “Olmo2: The object has been created, but the execution phase has not returned; release has not started.”
- “Olmo2: Execution output is available; the failure is in the cleanup phase.”
- “Nemotron: The report does not provide the actual call entry point; the Olmo2 test case has not been used to reproduce it.”
- “Nemotron: Located before model selection; construction has not yet started.”
- “Nemotron: Construction has started; subsequent phases still need to be confirmed using the actual entry point.”

These records serve to preserve boundaries, not to replace the original error. The original error should still be stored together with the corresponding call location. If there is only a verbal description and no entry point, a short record can initially be filed under Nemotron or Olmo, but do not specify a constructor, file, or cause of failure.

## Order for reviewing the Olmo2 file

After opening `packages/transformers/tests/models/olmo2/test_modeling_olmo2.js`, there is no need to read the entire test file in one go. Just stop at the following points in order:

1. First, look at the usage sites of `GPT2Tokenizer` and `Olmo2ForCausalLM` to confirm which object is affected by the symptoms in this instance.
2. Next, check whether the test uses `DEFAULT_MODEL_OPTIONS` and whether there are any local overrides visible at the call site.
3. Compare `MAX_MODEL_LOAD_TIME`, `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME`, and `MAX_MODEL_DISPOSE_TIME` to determine which phase was the last to complete.
4. If there was no model object before the failure, do not continue inspecting execution inputs.
5. If execution has finished, do not go back and describe the exception as a loading issue.
6. If only release remains incomplete, record the cleanup phase separately; do not extend this into a conclusion about model support.

This order is more reliable than inferring the model name from the error text. The test file provides a specific observation point for Olmo2; it does not bear the responsibility of proving anything about the entire model directory.

## Parallel handling of the two types of reports

Sometimes descriptions of Nemotron and Olmo exceptions arrive in the same round. In that case, a phase table can be shared, but results must not be shared:

| Model side | Available entry point | First thing to confirm | Material that must not be borrowed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Olmo | `test_modeling_olmo2.js` | The first test phase entered after import | Conclusions about Nemotron construction or execution |
| Nemotron | The location actually reached in the report | Whether model selection has completed | Olmo2 test results and default options |

“Available entry point” does not mean Olmo is already fully covered. It only means there is currently a path that can be reviewed. When Nemotron does not list a file, the blank should not be filled in with any seemingly reasonable directory.

Even if both types of reports manifest as timeouts, first split them by stage. Olmo stopping at the loading boundary and Nemotron stopping at the execution boundary are different symptoms; even if neither produces any output, they should not be merged into the same issue. Conversely, if both sides have finished execution and stop only during release, “cleanup phase” can be used as a shared observation, but their respective entry points must still be retained.

## When to Stop

The following situations should stop further narrowing rather than prompt a fabricated explanation:

- Nemotron has no actual hit at a construction, call, or test location.
- The Olmo record can confirm only the import, not the first failure after the import.
- The original exception does not indicate whether a model object was ever created.
- The test shows only the total elapsed time and does not indicate whether it stopped during loading, execution, or release.
- The default options were changed temporarily, but the original conditions were not preserved.

Stopping does not mean the exception has disappeared. It means the current material supports conclusions only up to this boundary. For Olmo, when raw output is available next time, continue from the actual usage point of `test_modeling_olmo2.js`; for Nemotron, first restore the actual entry point, then proceed with model-side investigation.

## Follow-up Notes

If follow-up records need to be added, do not rewrite all the branches on this page. Add only one line under the corresponding model and stage: the actual hit file or call location, the last successful stage, the first failure location, and whether release was entered. If the result overturns an earlier judgment, retain the old judgment and mark beside it that it no longer applies. In particular, do not write the old shortcut “Olmo2 is the Nemotron entry point” back into the document.

There are currently only two incomplete items: Nemotron’s local hit entry point, and a field sample from the Olmo2 test that can reliably identify the first failure stage. All other branches should still be handled according to the stage divisions above.

# CLI Parsing Trial Plan

For this round of interface review, proceed on the assumption that the parsing layer will not grow into a separate subsystem. CLI is responsible only for collecting command-line values; object construction will still go through the existing entry point. Otherwise, prerelease testing will have two sets of defaults and two error paths, making it hard for regression testing to determine whether differences come from argument interpretation or processor loading.

The place available for a lightweight check is `packages/transformers/tests/models/jina_clip/test_processor_jina_clip.js`. The file directly imports `AutoProcessor`, `JinaCLIPProcessor` and `load_cached_image`, and uses `MAX_PROCESSOR_LOAD_TIME` and `MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME`. This looks more like a processor test, so it should not be used as grounds for classifying CLI under JinaCLIP; however, we can reuse its loading time limit to first observe whether command-line arguments introduce extra waiting in the processor initialization path.

Start by trying two narrow paths: one that passes only explicit model or resource arguments, and one that uses defaults throughout. Pass the parsed result as a plain object to the existing entry point, without adding model-type branches in this layer. Callers are responsible for avoiding mutually exclusive arguments for now; if constraints on argument combinations are actually needed later, consider adding group definitions in the parsing layer then.

Rollback criteria: if the default and explicit paths select different processors, or the parsing layer starts duplicating resource cache logic, stop using this approach and return to handling each entry point separately.

To confirm: who maintains the help text; whether exceptions should be raised unchanged or rewritten at CLI.

# CLI Parsing Trial Plan

The initial idea was to keep the command-line layer very thin: read the options, pass them to the existing loading entry point, and keep it unaware of model directories, processor implementations, or resource caches. This judgment is retained because it explains why an independent argument object was not introduced immediately at the time; it also oversimplified one point—“thin” does not mean that all parameters can be combined freely.

## Tradeoffs Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft treated `packages/transformers/tests/models/jina_clip/test_processor_jina_clip.js` as a temporary observation point. The direct imports visible in that file are:

```js
import { AutoProcessor, JinaCLIPProcessor } from "../../../src/transformers.js";
import { load_cached_image } from "../../asset_cache.js";
import { MAX_PROCESSOR_LOAD_TIME, MAX_TEST_EXECUTION_TIME } from "../../init.js";
```

Based on this, we initially guessed that as long as the result of CLI ultimately still went through `AutoProcessor`, we could continue using the processor-loading time-limit checks to compare the differences. That guess was not sufficiently supported later: this test is adjacent to the JinaCLIP processor and image resources, not an implementation description that can replace the command-line entry point. The old proposal remains here because several discussions continued to rely on the claim that “processor tests cover parsing”; removing it would make the later disagreement look as if it appeared out of nowhere.

The smaller conclusion worth retaining is that parsed values should not reimplement resource reading at the CLI layer, and the processor should not be preloaded just to display help text. `load_cached_image` remains in the tests and resource paths and cannot become part of the CLI's default behavior.

## Trial Approach After Review

The creation notes for HFJ-217 require verifying CLI parsing in an environment without an old cache or personal configuration, and recording both newly created and not-created paths. The card also lists `add_argument`, `add_mutually_exclusive_group`, and `afmoe` as search terms. Subsequent work only confirmed that the card already had an owner; it left no record connecting these three names into a single implementation chain.

The trial therefore no longer targets “covering processor loading.” Instead, it first separates the parameter declarations themselves. The first batch permits only two types of declarations: single-value options and an explicitly mutually exclusive group of options. Single-value options are registered by `add_argument`; when two values cannot appear at the same time, use `add_mutually_exclusive_group`. This does not require writing a CLI branch for every model type. It is intended to prevent parameter names from quietly becoming aliases for the model registry.

The only call shape to retain is this layer:

```js
const parser = new ArgumentParser();
parser.add_argument("--model");
const source = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group();
const options = parser.parse_args();
```

The snippet above expresses the interface direction, not implemented code. In particular, `afmoe` should not be filled in with a parameter's default value; on the card, it is only a search term, not a default model that this proposal can confirm. The initial draft leaned toward putting the model type directly in the parsing layer; that part should now be treated as a deprecated working assumption.

The trial retains one old constraint: without an old cache or personal configuration, explicitly passed values and omitted values must be recorded separately. What is recorded here is the shape of the parsed object and whether it enters the loading entry point; processor execution time must not be used as a substitute for the parsing result. If a default appears only because of personal configuration, first treat its source as unclear rather than hard-coding it into the help text.

## Two Approaches Not Adopted

One approach was to have CLI recognize all model types directly and then select a processor or model constructor. It looks like it reduces steps in a demo, but it would make registry extensions require synchronized changes to the command-line layer; the existing material is insufficient to show that this layer can maintain that mapping over the long term. The other approach was to declare no mutual exclusions at all and leave conflicts to downstream errors. The initial draft leaned toward this because, with few parameters, it required the smallest change. After review, this is no longer recommended: once conflicting values enter the loading entry point, the resulting failure can no longer show what the user actually passed.

The cost of retaining mutually exclusive groups is that help output must be updated as group members change, and the caller must decide which options are actually mutually exclusive. This cost is smaller than maintaining a model-type table, but it is not zero, so use groups only for parameters with known conflicts; unconfirmed combinations should remain two ordinary options.

## Withdrawal and Open Items

If the parsing layer starts reading the cache, loading images, or constructing `JinaCLIPProcessor` in order to determine defaults, withdraw this trial. If mutually exclusive groups cannot express the actual parameter relationship, do not force the relationship with nested groups; revert to single-value declarations and pass the conflict to code closer to the business entry point.

The unresolved issue is not syntax but ownership of the defaults: should CLI fill them in, or should the downstream entry point do so? The existing review is sufficient only to narrow the issue to these two locations; it cannot decide between them.

# Postmortem: Two States for the Same Resource Site Object

The resource site's docs and guide originally served together as the user entry point, with version notes and outdated content handled under the same maintenance arrangements. During verification, the same “transformers · User Resource Site” object showed different current revisions at two points in time. The two sets of content were not treated as independent objects; they were first saved as two states of the same object during the investigation.

This first came to light when the ONNX manifest did not match the old record. The old record still opened, and the entry page still pointed to usable content, so it initially looked more like a delayed manifest update or version notes that had not been cleared somewhere. That assessment did not hold up: on another look, the conflict was not limited to one line in the manifest. The current entry point itself showed another current revision for the same object.

## Order of Observations

1. The old record came first. It preserved the resource site's entry-point state at the time, including the version information used for comparison with the ONNX manifest.
2. A different current revision was then seen through the current entry point. The object names in the two records were identical; renaming could not separate the discrepancy into different objects.
3. Repeated requests to the entry point were not continued during the investigation. The original record was retained, and the recovery page was kept separately so later entry-point changes would not overwrite the initial discrepancy.
4. The runtime version was later restored. This recovery only shows that the version field could return to a usable state; it does not show that the cause of the changes in partial content across the two observations had been found.

For a period in between, the work focused on whether the old manifest had not been synced. This was the working hypothesis at the time, not a confirmed attribution. The old manifest was indeed the first place the problem surfaced, but it could not explain why the same object showed two current revisions at two points in time. The review therefore did not list services outside the resource site, build processes, or adjacent projects as causes.

## Scope of Impact

The first impact was on maintenance decisions for the resource site: someone viewing the entry point could not determine which revision to use from the “current” label alone. Version notes and the handling of outdated content also could not be settled immediately because the entry-point states were inconsistent. The old record was not invalid; it documented a state that had actually appeared at an earlier point in time. Nor was the recovery page a replacement for the old record; it only preserved content that could be confirmed during recovery.

There was no evidence that all docs or guides were affected in the same way. The resource site had its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, but this record did not expand those management boundaries into technical causes. In particular, when both items are missing, the entry-point names alone cannot establish that they point to the same underlying content; this remained unknown during the investigation.

## Preservation and Stopping Point

The materials retained at the time were in `docs/adj-transformers/incidents/transformers-User Resource Site-Two States for the Same Object.md`. They should include the original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause, rather than only the runtime version restored later. The reason was straightforward: if the entry point changed again, the initially observed state could still be distinguished from the later recovery state.

Further retries were stopped not because the discrepancy had disappeared, but because continued reads from the same entry point would not fill two key gaps: when each different current revision appeared, and why the partial content changed. Without those two timestamps, a newly retrieved page could only represent a new state; it could not explain what had been observed during the investigation.

The reviewer retraced the original entry point and confirmed only that there was a real difference between the current entry point and the saved old record; branches that were not reproduced were not filled in as conclusions. The inconsistency in the ONNX manifest remained at the start of the timeline because it explained why verification began, but it was no longer treated as the sole cause.

## Still Open

- The times when the two current revisions appeared have not yet been established.
- The cause of the partial content changes has not been confirmed.
- The existing records are insufficient to determine whether the runtime version recovery was related to the entry-point state change.

If new original records are obtained later, append them after this incident and clearly identify which point in time each corresponds to; do not overwrite the old records or write the recovered entry-point state back into the initial observation.

# Reference Site Proposal Not Adopted

At the time, the idea was to separate `transformers-documentation-portal` from its place alongside the existing docs and guide entry points and make it a standalone entry point for users. The intent was not to replace the reference content, but to put version notes, handling of outdated content, and the user entry point on the same release path. Readers would no longer have to guess whether a section of the guide still applied to the version they were viewing; maintainers could also flag old content for retirement when version notes were added.

This approach was not adopted. The issue was not whether the pages could be built. Once the reference site became an entry point in its own right, two unresolved questions would have to be answered first: would the old docs remain a user entry point or serve only as an index, and would the existing version notes in the guide move or remain in both places? The former would leave people familiar with the old entry point suddenly unable to find content; the latter would leave maintainers manually keeping track of which notes were still valid. At the time, there was not enough confidence that the second option would be inexpensive to maintain.

Two approaches were provisionally compared:

- **Standalone reference site**: The reference site would take on the user entry point, version notes, and notices about outdated content; docs and guide would remain as content sources. The benefit was that entry points could be organized centrally by version. The cost was having to check where both sides pointed after every content change.
- **Keep the existing entry points**: Continue filling in the notes in docs and guide, keeping only navigation and archive locations for the reference site. This would not solve the problem of scattered entry points, but it would avoid introducing another layer of redirects before the content had stabilized.

The preference at the time was for the latter, so the standalone reference site was not scheduled for implementation. That judgment rested on one assumption: the existing entry points could still handle the volume of changes to version notes. If the same set of notes needed separate updates in docs, guide, and the reference site, or if retiring old content required manual page-by-page tracking, that assumption would no longer hold. At that point, reverse the decision not to split them yet and reopen discussion of a trial for a standalone entry point.

If the trial is reopened, start with only a small section of content that already has version notes; do not migrate the entire guide. Observe whether the reference site actually reduces how often readers have to compare entry points, and whether old content can be clearly flagged when versions change. The reference site must not become just another copy of the content; if it only adds a layer of links, stop the trial.

Still unresolved:

- Whether the old docs would still count as the primary user entry point after the reference site appeared;
- Whether outdated content would stay in place with a notice or move into an archive;
- Whether content maintainers would write version notes into the reference site or the notes would be collected as part of reference site maintenance.

The original draft is still at `docs/adj-transformers/proposals/not-adopted-transformers-user-reference-site-route.md`. This record preserves the trade-offs and reversal triggers for the approach that was not adopted at the time. Any later entry-point arrangements should be recorded separately, not written back as conclusions already reached in this discussion.

## Path Not Taken

When the next page's body is unavailable, record the page you are on and why you stopped. That makes it easier to reconstruct the trail on the next review than filling the gap with notes from a neighboring project.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy Review

During this maintenance window, the results shown by the team's public entry point did not match the original plan. The first thing observed was a discrepancy at the entry point, not an error in model loading itself; the incident notes initially linked the two too closely. That assessment is retained here to distinguish what was observable at the time from the actions later taken to restore visible results.

After the window started, maintenance proceeded as planned. When the issue was first noticed, the public entry point's results had not switched as planned. All that could be confirmed at the time was that the entry point's results were abnormal; it was not clear whether the issue lay in the model mapping, entry point configuration, or remnants of the old path. No signal was observed that could isolate any one of these three as the cause, so the entry point discrepancy was not recorded as an established runtime failure.

The model mapping diff from that time was then retrieved for comparison. The diff showed that the planned changes had indeed occurred, and that material had been available during the incident for later review; it did not explain why the public entry point was still returning the old results. The original notes treated the diff as the closest lead to the anomaly. It was later recognized that this conflated “the change exists” with “the entry point selected the change.” The notes remain on file in their original context.

The temporary response did not expand the mapping changes further. Instead, the old entry point was retained to restore visible results. The old entry point could be withdrawn, so this was an on-call recovery action, not confirmation of the mapping diff. After recovery, the same entry point no longer produced results that conflicted with the plan. The impact record was also limited to the public entry point layer; it was not used to infer that the model directory or runtime behavior had been affected.

During incident coordination, the record was split into three parts: the entry point behavior first observed, the old entry point retained to restore results, and the mapping diff, which could explain only part of the situation. This keeps handoffs from recording the recovery time as the point when the root cause became known, or mistaking the old entry point's presence for a long-term choice. If the same discrepancy appears again, first check the results actually returned by the entry point, then decide whether the diff needs to be reviewed.

Still unknown: why the old entry point continued to participate in result selection during the maintenance window; whether the discrepancy occurs only in this kind of public entry point maintenance; and whether it will recur after the temporary entry point is withdrawn. The original notes leaned toward classifying the issue as a mapping change that had not taken effect. That was the working assessment at the time, with insufficient evidence, and cannot serve as a conclusion for subsequent handling.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

This answer retains the early wording about the entry point because many old discussions left only the judgment that “the entry point is still there.” That judgment is useful for locating a candidate path, not for endorsing it; don't conflate what's displayed at the public entry point with a complete review.

The entry point here is more of a shared lookup location than a place to store results. It can show whether a candidate path is still referenced and whether its name is still available for discussion, but it doesn't combine baseline behavior, post-fix behavior, and post-withdrawal behavior into one record. For that reason, the old statement “the entry point is still there, so it has already been integrated” remains available as historical wording, but can no longer be used to close items.

**What does the existing generation-state entry point prove?**

It proves that maintainers still have a shared lookup location: the candidate path hasn't disappeared from the entry point, and its name is still available for discussion. The earlier answer described this step as “already integrated and ready to close.” A later on-site review found that this skipped the fix and withdrawal stages. The existence of the entry point is neither a record of baseline behavior nor a record that the fix has taken effect.

If all we confirm is that the name at the entry point hasn't changed, we can at most confirm that the candidate is still listed at the public entry point. We also need to run the same input through the existing path and the modified path to compare their actual behavior; checking again after withdrawal confirms that the entry point text is no longer endorsing the change. When results haven't been recorded separately for all three stages, this page does not interpret entry point status as completion status.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?**

The old draft said, “The entry point maintainer just needs to withdraw it.” That statement has no supporting basis and is retained as historical wording. Only two things have been confirmed: the party proposing the candidate path must explain the reason for withdrawal, and the entry point maintainer must also handle the reference at the entry point. There is no conclusion here on whether the same person performs both actions or who makes the final decision in a dispute. The entry point remaining visible does not mean someone has taken over responsibility for withdrawal.

So the party proposing the candidate path cannot leave only the word “withdrawn,” nor can they treat a missing reason as a decision by the entry point maintainer. The entry point maintainer handles the reference at the public entry point; the proposing party records the reason for withdrawal. The available records do not establish that both actions must be performed by the same person, nor do they identify an alternate decision-maker in a dispute.

**Under what conditions can the item be closed?**

The team's established practice is: only when the same input has produced reviewable results on the baseline, fixed, and rollback paths may the responsible person move the card into the release window. “The same input” is intended to prevent each stage from using a different sample and leaving conclusions that only appear consistent. The baseline preserves the original behavior, the fix records behavior after the change, and the rollback path confirms that removing the change hasn't left the judgment in the entry point text.

If any one of these three results is missing, checking the entry point can only serve as a lookup, not as a closure action. In particular, when the entry point text has already been changed, we still need to check whether the rollback path brings back the old judgment; the absence of the old wording on the page does not mean rollback is complete. Review results remain the basis for closure, rather than prematurely reducing that basis to what's displayed at the entry point.

Range probe records can be logged alongside the review, but this page has no evidence that they are required for closure. The old answer treated them as an ordinary supplement; that point wasn't confirmed in subsequent reviews and is not being added as a rule at this stage.

This review compared two approaches: retaining the existing generation-state entry point or adjusting the entry-point window at the current stage. The decision is to retain the existing entry point as a shared collaboration point; adjust the window only within the scope where the entry point, callers, and failure evidence can already be identified.

The old entry point is not removed by this decision. It should continue to be retained as a rollback path until a specific adjustment can explain the actual impact and the coordinator has collected the relevant records. The model directory name can help with tracing, but cannot by itself serve as the basis for adjusting the public entry point; the relevant call index is in DOC-01.
